claims.text: Five production-grade approaches to JSON-document drift / schema-diff are documented well enough to inform an MCP tools/list drift detector: oasdiff, OpenAPITools/openapi-diff, Buf protobuf breaking-change detection, Pact consumer-driven contract testing, and JSON Patch (RFC 6902) + JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785).
claims.notes: T-001 executive-summary synthesis claim; aggregates 5 surveyed approaches. Primary sources cited in note's source list rows 1-21.

claims.text: oasdiff implements a three-tier severity system across 450+ rules: ERR for definite breaking changes, WARN for potential ones not programmatically confirmable, and INFO for non-breaking changes.
claims.notes: Finding 1. Primary citation: oasdiff docs/BREAKING-CHANGES.md and oasdiff.com/docs/breaking-changes (T-001 source rows 1-2).

claims.text: Each oasdiff rule has a stable ID (e.g., endpoint-removed, request-property-removed, response-property-enum-value-added), and the severity per rule can be customized via --severity-levels.
claims.notes: Finding 1. Primary citation: oasdiff docs (T-001 source rows 1-2).

claims.text: oasdiff supports change fingerprints for stable cross-commit change identity, addressing the baseline-storage question.
claims.notes: Finding 1, verbatim phrase 'change fingerprints for stable cross-commit change identity'. Primary citation: oasdiff docs (T-001 source rows 1-2).

claims.text: The 450+ oasdiff rule catalog targets OpenAPI 3.x, not raw JSON Schema; mapping rules to tools/list's slim shape requires selection because most of oasdiff's 450 rules will not apply.
claims.notes: Finding 1 caveat. Author's analytical observation about transferability.

claims.text: In oasdiff, endpoint-removed and request-property-removed are ERR severity; response-optional-property-added is non-breaking; adding a required request param is ERR; adding an optional response field is INFO.
claims.notes: Finding 1 differentiated removal-vs-addition. Primary citation: oasdiff rule catalog (T-001 source rows 1-2).

claims.text: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff distinguishes two emit thresholds at the CLI level: --fail-on-changed (any structural change) and --fail-on-incompatible (only changes that break backward compatibility).
claims.notes: Finding 2. Primary citation: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff README (T-001 source row 3).

claims.text: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff's incompatibility taxonomy lives in BackwardIncompatibleProp, with explicit per-property toggles such as incompatible.response.enum.increased=false.
claims.notes: Finding 2. Primary citation: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff README (T-001 source row 3).

claims.text: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff 2.1.0 release notes document a concrete false-positive fix: removing an optional field from a response was previously incorrectly reported as a breaking change (PR #327).
claims.notes: Finding 2. Primary citation: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff 2.1.0 release notes (T-001 source row 4).

claims.text: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff Discussion #724 acknowledges the rule catalog is incomplete and proposes moving to a CSV-driven configuration table mirroring oasdiff's per-rule severity.
claims.notes: Finding 2 caveat. Primary citation: openapi-diff Discussion #724 (T-001 source row 5).

claims.text: OpenAPITools/openapi-diff Issue #673 confirms a known gap: removing or renaming response properties is not currently flagged as incompatible by the library's default rules.
claims.notes: Finding 2. Primary citation: openapi-diff Issue #673 (T-001 source row 6).

claims.text: Buf groups protobuf breaking-change rules into four strictly-nested categories from strictest to most lenient: FILE, PACKAGE, WIRE_JSON, WIRE, where passing a stricter category implies passing every looser one.
claims.notes: Finding 3. Primary citation: Buf docs 'Detecting breaking changes' and 'Rules and categories' (T-001 source rows 7, 9).

claims.text: Buf documents WIRE_JSON as the recommended minimum baseline because protobuf's JSON encoding breaks when field names change; WIRE only catches binary-encoding breakage.
claims.notes: Finding 3. Primary citation: Buf docs (T-001 source rows 7, 9).

claims.text: Buf's RPC_NO_DELETE rule explicitly flags RPC deletion as breaking and is included in FILE by default.
claims.notes: Finding 3 differentiated removal-vs-addition. Primary citation: Buf rules page (T-001 source row 9).

claims.text: Buf provides a configuration surface in buf.yaml with use, except, ignore, ignore_only, and ignore_unstable_packages directives for per-rule allowlisting.
claims.notes: Finding 3. Primary citation: Buf docs (T-001 source rows 7-10).

claims.text: Pact's default matcher behavior follows Postel's Law: JSON request bodies and query strings reject unexpected values, while JSON response bodies ignore unexpected values.
claims.notes: Finding 4. Primary citation: Pact docs 'Matching' and Pact-JVM matching guide (T-001 source rows 11-12).

claims.text: Pact matchers can be selected by JSON-Path with a documented weighting algorithm where more specific paths win over wildcard paths for the same target.
claims.notes: Finding 4. Example: $.body.item1.level[*].id (weight 32) wins over $.body.*.level[*].id (weight 8). Primary citation: Pact docs (T-001 source rows 11-13).

claims.text: Pact matchers include type (same JSON type, value ignored), regex (regex must match), arrayContaining (set membership, order-independent), eachKeyMatches, and atLeast/atMost for collection size.
claims.notes: Finding 4. Primary citation: Pact docs (T-001 source rows 11-13).

claims.text: Pact does not natively differentiate severity — a contract either passes or fails — but its asymmetry of strict-on-request / lenient-on-response is a primary-source endorsement of directionality.
claims.notes: Finding 4 differentiated removal-vs-addition. Primary citation: Pact docs (T-001 source rows 11-13).

claims.text: RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme, June 2020) defines a deterministic serialization that property-sorts JSON objects recursively in UTF-16 code-unit order, applies the I-JSON subset (RFC 7493), and uses ECMAScript-defined number serialization.
claims.notes: Finding 5a. Primary citation: IETF RFC 8785 (T-001 source row 16).

claims.text: JCS output is a byte-stable hashable representation: same input data produces the same canonical bytes across implementations.
claims.notes: Finding 5a. Primary citation: RFC 8785 (T-001 source row 16).

claims.text: JCS is normalization, not diffing — it gives a stable baseline for storage and hashing but downstream still requires a structural diff.
claims.notes: Finding 5a caveat. Author's analytical observation.

claims.text: JCS mandates UTF-16 sorting (not UTF-8); naive implementations using JSON.stringify with Object.keys().sort() get this wrong for non-BMP characters.
claims.notes: Finding 5a caveat. Primary citation: RFC 8785 (T-001 source row 16).

claims.text: RFC 6902 defines a stable JSON Patch diff vocabulary — add, remove, replace, move, copy, test — with JSON-Pointer (RFC 6901) paths.
claims.notes: Finding 5b. Primary citation: IETF RFC 6902 (T-001 source row 15).

claims.text: Production JSON Patch implementations (wI2L/jsondiff for Go, flipkart-incubator/zjsonpatch for Java) document specific algorithmic levers for false-positive control: LCS (longest common subsequence) to avoid spurious shift-induced replacements when an array element is deleted; Factorize() to coalesce removal+addition pairs into move operations; Ignores() to exclude JSON-Pointer paths from the diff; identity-based list diffing using a key field per array.
claims.notes: Finding 5b. Primary citation: wI2L/jsondiff README, flipkart-incubator/zjsonpatch README, java-json-tools/json-patch (T-001 source rows 17-19).

claims.text: RFC 6902 is a vocabulary, not a severity-classifier — it specifies what changed but not whether it is breaking.
claims.notes: Finding 5b caveat. Author's analytical observation about RFC 6902.

claims.text: In RFC 6902 vocabulary, op:"remove" vs op:"add" is a first-class structural distinction in the patch document, providing the cleanest direct representation of removal-vs-addition differentiation.
claims.notes: Finding 5b differentiated removal-vs-addition. Primary citation: RFC 6902 (T-001 source row 15).

claims.text: The MCP specification (2025-11-25) defines the tools/list response shape: each tool object carries name (required, unique), title (optional human-readable), description (optional human-readable, by design free-text and high-volatility), inputSchema (JSON Schema 2020-12 default), outputSchema (optional), icons (optional), annotations (optional), and execution.taskSupport.
claims.notes: Finding 6. Primary citation: MCP specification 2025-11-25 (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: The MCP tools capability declaration is "capabilities": {"tools": {"listChanged": true}}, and when the list changes servers SHOULD emit notifications/tools/list_changed.
claims.notes: Finding 6. Primary citation: MCP specification 2025-11-25 (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: Servers that support tools MUST declare the tools capability per the MCP specification.
claims.notes: Finding 6 verbatim quote from MCP spec. Primary citation: MCP specification 2025-11-25 (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: The MCP 2024-11-05 spec lacked the title, icons, annotations, and execution fields; multi-version-aware diffing must tolerate optional-field absence vs presence on the same server across protocol upgrades.
claims.notes: Finding 6 caveat. Primary citation: MCP specification (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: MCP SEP-2549 is a draft TTL-for-list-results proposal that, if accepted, will add ttlMs and cacheScope fields to the tools/list response shape.
claims.notes: Finding 6 caveat. Primary citation: MCP SEP-2549 (T-001 source row 21).

claims.text: The MCP description field is explicitly described as 'Human-readable description of functionality' — free-text and by design volatile, such that a naive byte-diff against this field will produce false positives on every documentation polish.
claims.notes: Finding 6 normalization rationale. Primary citation: MCP specification (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: A defensible architecture for the MCP tools/list drift detector is a four-stage pipeline: (1) normalize the response with JCS (RFC 8785) or equivalent property-sorted canonical form; (2) persist baseline as the JCS-canonical bytes; (3) diff with RFC 6902 (JSON Patch) using LCS for array comparisons and identity-based list diffing keyed on name; (4) classify each patch operation against a per-rule severity catalog modeled on oasdiff.
claims.notes: Synthesis claim — author's own composition; not from any one source. Cites underlying primaries: RFC 8785 (JCS), RFC 6902 (JSON Patch), oasdiff (severity), MCP spec (name as identity key). T-001 source rows 1, 15, 16, 20.

claims.text: In the recommended classification catalog: remove at /tools/<name> is high severity; add at /tools/<name> is medium severity; replace anywhere under /tools/<name>/inputSchema or /tools/<name>/outputSchema is high severity; replace at /tools/<name>/description or /tools/<name>/title is informational; replace at /tools/<name>/icons or /tools/<name>/annotations is informational.
claims.notes: Synthesis recommendation by T-001 author for AC-FR-5 mapping; not verbatim from any one source.

claims.text: The crucial false-positive-suppression move for tools/list drift detection is not in the diff algorithm — it is in normalization (which removes structural noise) and severity catalog routing (which routes description-drift to INFO).
claims.notes: Synthesis conclusion by T-001 author.

claims.text: Pure-structural diff tools like RFC 6902 by itself detect what changed faithfully but cannot decide severity; pure-semantic tools like Buf and oasdiff bake in opinions that may or may not match a specific project's acceptance criteria — a PRD-controlled severity table is the bridge.
claims.notes: Synthesis trade-off: semver-awareness vs. structural-equality. Author's analytical observation.

claims.text: Ignoring the description field entirely suppresses noise but risks missing a description that encodes signature-relevant info — some MCP tool implementations document required input formats only in description.
claims.notes: Synthesis trade-off: description-text noise vs. signature-change false negatives. Author's analytical observation.

claims.text: Naive JSON-diff on tools (an array) treats any reordering as a wholesale replacement, which is a classic false-positive driver; identity-keyed list diffing using the tool name field gives per-tool change identity that survives reordering.
claims.notes: Synthesis trade-off: whole-array replacement vs. granular per-tool diff. Author's analytical observation.

claims.text: For an audit tool that must meet specified ACs exactly, the diff/severity rules must be enumerated locally and reviewed against those ACs, not inherited from a third-party default; OpenAPITools/openapi-diff Issue #673 is a cautionary tale of a maintained library carrying defaults that miss real breaking changes.
claims.notes: Synthesis trade-off: defaults vs. configurability. Cites openapi-diff Issue #673 (T-001 source row 6).

claims.text: The MCP spec's notifications/tools/list_changed event surface is SHOULD-strength (not MUST), and a server may legitimately drift without firing it (e.g., server restart with new code); a polled, snapshot-based audit is more reliable than a notification-listener for drift detection.
claims.notes: Synthesis trade-off: notification-driven vs. polled audit. Primary citation: MCP specification (T-001 source row 20).

claims.text: A < 5% false-positive target for drift detection is empirically achievable when: normalization (JCS) eliminates non-semantic noise before the diff runs; array comparison uses identity keys (tool name) not positional index; the severity catalog is enumerated locally; and free-text fields like description and title are routed to INFO severity, not suppressed.
claims.notes: Synthesis conclusion by T-001 author about PRD NFR-4 achievability.

claims.text: 50 audits against a stable upstream still encompass the upstream's own minor description polishing and icon-URL CDN rewrites — these appear as patch operations, so a naive any-diff-equals-positive classifier will exceed 5% FP, while a catalog-driven classifier reads them as INFO and they correctly do not count as false positives against a WARN-or-stricter threshold.
claims.notes: Synthesis failure-mode warning by T-001 author.

claims.text: No surveyed primary source publishes a quantitative false-positive-rate benchmark for JSON drift / schema diff (no library publishes a metric of the form 'our drift detector achieves X% FP under Y normalization regime').
claims.notes: T-001 load-bearing negative finding (open question 1). The < 5% PRD target must be measured during implementation, not inherited from a published number.

claims.text: No surveyed primary source covers MCP-specific drift detection; the MCP specification provides the wire shape but not the drift-detection algorithm, and the surveyed approaches all target adjacent domains (OpenAPI, protobuf, generic JSON, contract testing).
claims.notes: T-001 open question 2. Negative observation about the MCP niche.

claims.text: The MCP 2025-11-25 spec warns: clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, implying that an annotation-drift event has different severity depending on the server's trust posture.
claims.notes: T-001 open question 3 (annotation-trust boundary). Primary citation: MCP specification 2025-11-25 (T-001 source row 20).
